title: Anatomy, physiology and genetics of pregnancy and fetal development
blurb: Explain the normal changes of pregnancy in each body system, trace the fetal circulation and its shunts, and use basic genetics to explain screening.
question: Priya is 30 weeks pregnant. She is breathless climbing stairs, has heartburn after meals, and felt faint lying flat on her back for a scan. Her haemoglobin has fallen since booking. Which of these are normal adaptations, and why?

teach.body: To grow a baby and prepare for blood loss at birth, the woman's body changes in every system, driven largely by progesterone, oestrogen and placental hormones. A midwife must know these normal changes so she can reassure, and so she can spot a deviation from normal that needs referral (SPM 3.23, 3.26). In plain English: know what 'normal pregnant' looks like, and anything outside it stands out.
teach.cite: Soma-Pillay et al., Cardiovasc J Afr 2016;27(2):89–94

teach.body: In late pregnancy, lying flat on her back lets the uterus press on the inferior vena cava and aorta. Turning from lateral to supine can cut cardiac output by about 25%, reducing placental blood flow. So women are cared for in the left or right lateral position where possible, or with the uterus displaced if she must lie on her back. This is also why, in maternal collapse after 20 weeks, the uterus is displaced manually to the left.

teach.h: Genetics and epigenetics in a sentence each
teach.body: Genetics: humans have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs; a trisomy is an extra copy, as in Down's (21), Edwards' (18) and Patau's (13) syndromes that FASP screens for. When both parents carry a recessive condition such as sickle cell disease, each baby has a 1 in 4 chance of being affected, which is why the baby's father is offered testing if the woman is a carrier. Epigenetics: environmental factors such as smoking and nutrition change how genes are expressed without changing the DNA sequence.

teach.body: Priya's breathlessness on stairs (bigger tidal volume), heartburn (lower sphincter tone) and lower Hb (dilution) can all be normal, so the midwife reassures her while checking her Hb result against local anaemia thresholds. Feeling faint on her back is aortocaval compression: she should rest on her side. If her BP were 145/95 or she was breathless at rest, that would be a deviation needing referral.

teach.text: A lower Hb in pregnancy is often dilution, not iron deficiency: the red cell indices (MCV, MCHC) do not fall as they do in iron deficiency. And because BP normally FALLS mid-pregnancy, a first reading of 140/90 or more after 20 weeks is not a normal adaptation: refer to be seen in secondary care within 24 hours (NICE NG201 1.2.26).

items: Plasma volume rises about 50% and red cells less, so Hb falls by dilution.
Cardiac output rises about 40%, mostly from stroke volume; heart rate rises 10–20 bpm; SVR falls 25–30%.
BP dips in the first two trimesters and returns to baseline in the third.
Supine position can cut cardiac output by about 25%: use lateral positions.
Insulin resistance rises from the second trimester, which is why GDM testing is at 24–28 weeks.
Fetal shunts (ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus) bypass liver and lungs and close after birth.

summary: You can now explain the main cardiovascular, blood, respiratory, renal, gastrointestinal and metabolic changes of pregnancy and use them to tell normal from abnormal. You can also trace the fetal circulation and its three shunts, and apply basic genetics to screening conversations.

A.q: Why does haemoglobin concentration usually fall in a healthy pregnancy?
options: Red cell production stops in pregnancy
Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass
Red cells are destroyed faster than usual
A.why: Plasma volume rises by about 50%, more than red cell mass, so Hb concentration falls by haemodilution.

whyNot.0: Red cell mass actually increases in pregnancy, just less than plasma.
whyNot.2: The fall is due to dilution, not marrow suppression.
whyNot.3: Increased red cell breakdown is not the normal mechanism.

A.q: Cardiac output rises by about 40% in pregnancy. What mainly causes this rise?
options: A rise in heart rate of around 40 bpm
A rise in systemic vascular resistance
A fall in circulating plasma volume
A.why: The rise is achieved predominantly by an increase in stroke volume, with a smaller rise in heart rate (10–20 bpm).

whyNot.0: Heart rate rises by only 10–20 bpm.

A.q: In the fetal circulation, which shunt carries blood from the pulmonary artery into the descending aorta?
A.why: Most right ventricular output passes through the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta, bypassing the fluid-filled lungs.

whyNot.0: The ductus venosus diverts umbilical venous blood past the liver to the IVC.
whyNot.1: The foramen ovale connects the right and left atria.
whyNot.2: The umbilical vein brings oxygen-rich blood from the placenta.

B.q: Abi, 33 weeks, feels faint and clammy while lying flat on her back for a scan. What should the midwife do first?
options: Turn her onto her left side
Raise her legs while she lies flat
Tilt her flat with her head down
Give oxygen and keep her flat
B.why: This is aortocaval compression: lying supine can cut cardiac output by about 25%. A lateral position relieves pressure on the vena cava.

whyNot.1: Keeping her supine leaves the uterus compressing the vena cava.
whyNot.2: Head-down supine keeps the compression and is uncomfortable.
whyNot.3: Oxygen does not relieve the cause; she needs to come off her back.

B.q: Why are pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria at increased risk of pyelonephritis?
B.why: Progesterone reduces ureteric tone and peristalsis, dilating the collecting system (physiological hydronephrosis) and causing urinary stasis.

whyNot.3: Bladder neck tightening is not the mechanism.

B.q: Which describes the normal pattern of blood pressure across pregnancy?
options: Rises steadily through pregnancy and peaks at term
Falls in the first two trimesters, then returns
Stays unchanged from booking until the birth
Falls steadily from booking until the birth
B.why: BP decreases in the first and second trimesters (falling vascular resistance) and returns to non-pregnant levels in the third trimester.

whyNot.0: A steady rise is not normal and may signal hypertension.
whyNot.2: BP does change: it dips mid-pregnancy.
whyNot.3: BP returns to baseline in the third trimester.

C.q: Why are women at risk of gestational diabetes offered an oral glucose tolerance test at 24–28 weeks rather than at booking?
options: Fasting glucose peaks in the first trimester
Glucose spills into urine after 24 weeks
Insulin resistance rises from the second trimester
C.why: Placental and other hormones cause insulin resistance that starts in the second trimester and peaks in the third, unmasking GDM.

whyNot.0: Fasting glucose actually falls in pregnancy.
whyNot.2: Urine glucose is not used to assess GDM risk (NICE NG3).

C.q: Priya is 30 weeks pregnant. Which finding is a deviation from normal that needs referral?
options: Pulse 12 bpm above her booking rate
C.why: BP normally falls mid-pregnancy; a first episode of 140/90 or more after 20 weeks needs referral to be seen within 24 hours (NICE NG201 1.2.26).

whyNot.0: Exertional breathlessness fits the normal rise in tidal volume.
whyNot.1: Heartburn fits reduced lower oesophageal sphincter tone.
whyNot.3: A rise of 10–20 bpm is a normal adaptation.

C.q: At birth, what happens to the fetal circulation as the baby breathes and the placenta separates?
options: The shunts close as lung blood flow rises
The ductus venosus starts supplying the lungs
The foramen ovale opens to fill the lungs
The umbilical vein carries blood to the placenta
C.why: As the lungs expand, pulmonary blood flow rises sharply, the placenta detaches and the shunts close over minutes to hours.

whyNot.1: The ductus venosus links the umbilical vein and IVC; it does not supply the lungs.
whyNot.2: The foramen ovale closes after birth; it does not open.
whyNot.3: The umbilical vein carries blood from, not to, the placenta, and stops after birth.

reteach.title: More volume, less resistance
reteach.question: If you remember one sentence about the pregnant circulation, which should it be?

blocks.body: Vessels relax (resistance down about 25–30%), so the body fills them with more plasma (up about 50%) and pumps harder (cardiac output up about 40%, mostly bigger beats). Everything else follows: Hb dilutes, BP dips then recovers, and a heavy uterus on the vena cava can drop output when she lies flat.

blocks.text: Supine faintness in late pregnancy is aortocaval compression. The fix is position (lateral), not fluids or oxygen.

explain.body: Plasma volume up about 50%, cardiac output up about 40% (mostly stroke volume), heart rate up 10–20 bpm, SVR down 25–30%. Clotting factors rise: pregnancy is hypercoagulable.

test.q: Why is pregnancy described as a hypercoagulable state?
options: Plasma volume falls in late pregnancy
Red cell mass doubles by term
test.why: Clotting factors, particularly VIII, IX and X, and fibrinogen increase, preparing for haemostasis after birth and raising VTE risk.

whyNot.0: Platelet counts tend to fall slightly in pregnancy.
whyNot.3: Red cell mass rises, but far less than doubling.

explain.body: Respiratory: bigger tidal volume, mild compensated respiratory alkalosis. Renal: GFR up 50–85%, ureters dilated by progesterone. Gut: lower oesophageal sphincter tone falls, causing reflux.

test.q: What causes the increased breathing (hyperventilation) of normal pregnancy?
options: A rise in arterial carbon dioxide
test.why: Maternal hyperventilation comes from a larger tidal volume rather than a faster rate, lowering arterial carbon dioxide.

whyNot.0: Respiratory rate changes little; tidal volume rises.
whyNot.3: Arterial carbon dioxide falls in pregnancy.

explain.body: Oxygen-rich blood arrives in the umbilical vein. The ductus venosus bypasses the liver, the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the lungs, and the umbilical arteries return blood to the placenta.

test.q: Which fetal structure allows blood to bypass the liver?
test.why: The ductus venosus diverts part of the umbilical venous blood past the liver into the inferior vena cava.

whyNot.0: The foramen ovale bypasses the lungs at atrial level.
whyNot.1: The ductus arteriosus bypasses the lungs at arterial level.
whyNot.3: The umbilical arteries carry blood back to the placenta.

explain.body: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Trisomy = an extra chromosome (21, 18, 13). Two carriers of a recessive condition have a 1 in 4 chance with each pregnancy of an affected baby. Epigenetics changes gene expression without changing DNA.

test.q: Both parents carry the sickle cell gene. What is the chance, in each pregnancy, that the baby has sickle cell disease?
test.why: Sickle cell disease is recessive: with two carrier parents each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of an affected baby, 1 in 2 of a carrier and 1 in 4 of neither.

whyNot.0: 1 in 2 is the chance the baby is a carrier.
whyNot.2: 3 in 4 is the chance the baby is NOT affected.
